fr.title: Histoire du prophète Youssouf, d’après le Coran
fr.metaTitle: Histoire du prophète Youssouf, d’après le Coran
fr.metaDesc: Le rêve, le puits, la prison, puis l’Égypte : l’histoire du prophète Youssouf telle que le Coran la raconte, dans la sourate qui porte son nom.
fr.ex: Le rêve, le puits, la prison, puis le pardon : l’histoire de Youssouf telle que la raconte sa sourate.
fr.body:
La sourate Youssouf, le douzième chapitre du Coran, raconte une seule histoire en 111 versets. C’est celle du prophète Youssouf, Yūsuf en arabe, que la Bible appelle Joseph. Juste avant de la raconter, le Coran dit au Prophète Muhammad ﷺ : « Nous te racontons le plus beau des récits. »

Le rêve des onze étoiles

Youssouf est un jeune garçon. Son père, Yacoub, que la Bible appelle Jacob, est lui aussi un prophète. Youssouf lui raconte un rêve.

إِذۡ قَالَ يُوسُفُ لِأَبِيهِ يَٰٓأَبَتِ إِنِّي رَأَيۡتُ أَحَدَ عَشَرَ كَوۡكَبࣰا وَٱلشَّمۡسَ وَٱلۡقَمَرَ رَأَيۡتُهُمۡ لِي سَٰجِدِينَ

« Père, j’ai vu onze étoiles, le soleil et la lune s’incliner jusqu’au sol devant moi. »

Yacoub lui répond : « Ne raconte pas ton rêve à tes frères, ils pourraient comploter contre toi. » Il ajoute qu’Allah va le choisir et lui apprendre à expliquer les rêves (12:6).

Le Prophète Muhammad ﷺ a dit de cette famille : « Le noble, fils du noble, fils du noble, fils du noble : Youssouf, fils de Yacoub, fils d’Ishaq, fils d’Ibrahim » (al-Bukhārī, n° 3390). Ishaq est Isaac, et Ibrahim est Abraham. Le recueil d’al-Bukhārī réunit des hadiths, les paroles du Prophète ﷺ, que les savants tiennent pour authentiques.

Le puits et la chemise

Youssouf a d’autres frères, et ils sont jaloux : « Youssouf et son frère sont plus aimés de notre père que nous. » Ce frère est un autre fils de Yacoub, que la sourate ne nomme pas. Certains veulent tuer Youssouf. L’un d’eux propose plutôt un puits, où des voyageurs le trouveront (12:10).

Les frères obtiennent de Yacoub que Youssouf vienne courir et jouer avec eux, malgré sa peur d’un loup (12:11-13). Ils le descendent au fond d’un puits. Là, Allah fait savoir à Youssouf : « Un jour, tu leur rappelleras ce qu’ils ont fait, et ils ne te reconnaîtront pas. »

Le soir, les frères rentrent en pleurant, avec sa chemise tachée d’un faux sang : un loup l’aurait dévoré. Yacoub ne les croit pas : « Non, vous vous êtes laissé tenter par une mauvaise action. Il me reste une belle patience, et c’est Allah que j’appelle à l’aide. » Une belle patience, expliquent les commentateurs, reste calme et ne se plaint pas aux gens.

Des voyageurs passent près du puits. L’un d’eux descend son seau et s’écrie : « Bonne nouvelle ! Voici un garçon ! » Ils emmènent Youssouf et le vendent pour quelques pièces (12:20).

La maison du ʿAzīz, puis la prison

En Égypte, un haut dignitaire achète Youssouf. La sourate l’appelle le ʿAzīz, « le puissant ». Youssouf grandit dans sa maison, et Allah lui donne sagesse et savoir (12:21-22).

La femme du ʿAzīz veut le séduire. Elle ferme les portes, mais Youssouf refuse : « Qu’Allah me protège ! » Il court vers la porte. Elle le retient, et sa chemise se déchire dans le dos. Devant son mari, elle accuse Youssouf. Un homme de sa famille à elle tranche : une chemise déchirée dans le dos prouve que Youssouf dit vrai. Le mari donne raison à Youssouf (12:25-29).

Les femmes de la ville en parlent. La femme du ʿAzīz les invite et fait entrer Youssouf. En le voyant, elles se coupent les mains avec leurs couteaux : « Ce n’est pas un être humain, c’est un ange noble ! »

La femme du ʿAzīz le menace de prison. Youssouf dit à Allah : « Seigneur, la prison m’est plus chère que ce qu’elles me demandent. » Il est emprisonné, alors que son innocence est connue (12:32-35).

En prison, deux jeunes hommes lui racontent leurs rêves. Il leur parle d’abord d’Allah, le seul à adorer, puis les explique (12:36-41). Il demande à celui qui va être libéré de parler de lui au roi. Mais le Diable le lui fait oublier, et Youssouf reste en prison plusieurs années (12:42).

Le rêve du roi et les années de famine

Le roi d’Égypte rêve de sept vaches grasses mangées par sept vaches maigres, et de sept épis verts près de sept épis secs (12:43). Personne ne sait l’expliquer. L’homme sorti de prison se souvient alors de Youssouf (12:45).

Youssouf l’explique. Sept années de bonnes récoltes vont venir : il faudra garder le grain dans ses épis. Suivront sept années dures, où l’on vivra de ces réserves. Puis une année de pluie apportera le soulagement (12:47-49).

Le roi le fait appeler, mais Youssouf veut d’abord que son innocence soit établie (12:50). Le Prophète ﷺ a salué cette patience : « Si j’étais resté en prison aussi longtemps que Youssouf, j’aurais répondu à celui qui m’appelait » (al-Bukhārī, n° 3372, et Muslim, n° 151).

La femme du ʿAzīz avoue : « C’est moi qui ai voulu le séduire, et lui dit vrai. » Le roi en fait son proche conseiller, puis lui confie, à sa demande, les réserves du pays (12:54-56).

Ses frères reviennent : « Pas de reproche contre vous aujourd’hui »

Pendant les années dures, les fils de Yacoub viennent en Égypte acheter du grain. Youssouf les reconnaît, mais eux ne le reconnaissent pas (12:58). Il leur demande de revenir avec leur frère resté chez leur père (12:59).

Yacoub hésite, car il a déjà perdu Youssouf, puis il accepte (12:64-66). En Égypte, Youssouf dit en secret à ce frère : « Je suis ton frère. Ne sois pas triste. » Puis il fait cacher la coupe du roi dans son sac : selon la règle que les frères ont eux-mêmes donnée, celui qui l’a doit rester. Youssouf garde ainsi son frère (12:70-76).

Les autres rentrent sans lui. Yacoub répond encore par une belle patience (12:83), mais sa peine pour Youssouf lui blanchit les yeux (12:84). Il dit : « Je ne me plains de ma peine qu’à Allah. » Puis il renvoie ses fils chercher Youssouf et son frère, sans désespérer de la miséricorde d’Allah (12:87).

De retour en Égypte, les frères entendent Youssouf leur demander ce qu’ils ont fait à Youssouf et à son frère (12:89). Ils comprennent : « Es-tu Youssouf ? » Il répond : « Je suis Youssouf, et voici mon frère. » Ils reconnaissent leur faute (12:91), et Youssouf leur dit :

قَالَ لَا تَثۡرِيبَ عَلَيۡكُمُ ٱلۡيَوۡمَۖ يَغۡفِرُ ٱللَّهُ لَكُمۡۖ وَهُوَ أَرۡحَمُ ٱلرَّٰحِمِينَ

« Pas de reproche contre vous aujourd’hui. Qu’Allah vous pardonne. Il est le plus miséricordieux de ceux qui font miséricorde. »

Il leur confie sa chemise. Posée sur le visage de Yacoub, elle lui rend la vue (12:93-96). Ses fils lui demandent d’implorer le pardon d’Allah pour eux, et il le promet (12:97-98).

Toute la famille vient en Égypte. Youssouf installe ses parents sur le trône, et tous s’inclinent devant lui, un salut de respect à l’époque selon les commentateurs. Youssouf dit : « Père, voici le sens de mon rêve d’autrefois. » Les onze étoiles étaient ses frères, le soleil et la lune ses parents.

Dans cette joie, Youssouf parle de la prison, mais pas du puits. Il dit seulement que le Diable avait semé la discorde « entre moi et mes frères ». Le commentateur as-Saʿdī y voit un pardon complet, sans un mot de reproche.

Ce que la sourate ne dit pas

La sourate ne nomme ni les frères de Youssouf ni la femme du ʿAzīz. Elle ne dit ni l’âge de Youssouf, ni la couleur de sa chemise, ni combien de temps il est resté dans le puits. Les noms et les détails qu’on lit ailleurs viennent de récits plus tardifs, qui ne remontent à aucun témoin sûr. Cet article s’en tient au Coran et aux hadiths authentiques, comme l’histoire de la sourate al-Fīl.

Dans l’appli Nūr, les Histoires racontent une partie de cette sourate, le rêve, le puits et la chemise, sous le titre « La chemise et le loup ».

en.title: Story of Prophet Yusuf, as the Quran Tells It
en.metaTitle: Story of Prophet Yusuf, as the Quran Tells It
en.metaDesc: The dream, the well, the prison, then Egypt: the story of Prophet Yusuf as the Quran tells it, in the surah named after him.
en.ex: The dream, the well, the prison and finally forgiveness: Yūsuf’s story as the surah named after him tells it.
en.body:
Surah Yusuf, the twelfth chapter of the Quran, tells a single story across 111 verses: the story of the Prophet Yūsuf, known in the Bible as Joseph. Just before it begins, the Quran says to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: “We tell you the most beautiful of stories.”

The dream of the eleven stars

Yūsuf was a young boy. His father, Yaʿqūb, known in the Bible as Jacob, was also a prophet. Yūsuf told him about a dream.

إِذۡ قَالَ يُوسُفُ لِأَبِيهِ يَٰٓأَبَتِ إِنِّي رَأَيۡتُ أَحَدَ عَشَرَ كَوۡكَبࣰا وَٱلشَّمۡسَ وَٱلۡقَمَرَ رَأَيۡتُهُمۡ لِي سَٰجِدِينَ

“Father, I saw eleven stars, and the sun and the moon, bow down to the ground before me.”

Yaʿqūb replied: “Do not tell your dream to your brothers, or they may plot against you.” He added that Allah would choose him and teach him how to interpret dreams (12:6).

The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ described this family in these words: “The noble, son of the noble, son of the noble, son of the noble: Yūsuf, son of Yaʿqūb, son of Isḥāq, son of Ibrāhīm” (al-Bukhārī, no. 3390). Isḥāq is Isaac, and Ibrāhīm is Abraham. Al-Bukhārī’s book is a collection of hadiths, the sayings of the Prophet ﷺ, which scholars hold to be authentic.

The well and the shirt

Yūsuf had other brothers, and they were jealous: “Yūsuf and his brother are dearer to our father than we are.” The brother they mention was another son of Yaʿqūb. The surah doesn’t name him. Some of them wanted to kill Yūsuf. One suggested putting him in a well instead, where travellers would find him (12:10).

The brothers talked Yaʿqūb into letting Yūsuf go out with them to run and play, although he was afraid a wolf might eat the boy (12:11-13). They lowered him to the bottom of a well. There, Allah made this known to him: “One day you will tell them what they did, and they will not know it is you.”

That evening the brothers came home in tears, carrying his shirt stained with false blood. A wolf had eaten him, they said. Yaʿqūb didn’t believe them: “No, you have talked yourselves into a wrong deed. What is left to me is beautiful patience, and Allah is the One I ask for help.” Beautiful patience, the commentators explain, means staying calm and not complaining to people.

Some travellers came by the well. One of them lowered his bucket and called out: “Good news! Here is a boy!” They took Yūsuf and sold him for a few coins (12:20).

The house of the ʿAzīz, then prison

In Egypt, a high official bought Yūsuf. The surah calls him the ʿAzīz, “the mighty one”. Yūsuf grew up in his house, and Allah gave him wisdom and knowledge (12:21-22).

The ʿAzīz’s wife tried to seduce him. She shut the doors, but Yūsuf refused: “I seek refuge in Allah!” He ran for the door. She caught hold of him, and his shirt tore at the back. Then, in front of her husband, she accused Yūsuf. A man from her own family settled the matter: the tear at the back showed that Yūsuf was telling the truth. Her husband believed Yūsuf (12:25-29).

The women of the city began to gossip. The ʿAzīz’s wife invited them and called Yūsuf in. When they saw him, they cut their hands with their knives: “This is no human being. This is a noble angel!”

The ʿAzīz’s wife threatened him with prison. Yūsuf said to Allah: “My Lord, prison is dearer to me than what they ask of me.” He was locked up, even though they knew he was innocent (12:32-35).

In prison, two young men told him their dreams. He spoke to them first about Allah, the One who alone deserves worship, and then interpreted their dreams (12:36-41). He asked the one who was about to be freed to mention him to the king. But Satan made the man forget, and Yūsuf stayed in prison for several years (12:42).

The king’s dream and the years of famine

The king of Egypt dreamt of seven fat cows being eaten by seven thin ones, and of seven green ears of grain beside seven dry ones (12:43). No one could interpret it. Then the man who had been freed from prison remembered Yūsuf (12:45).

Yūsuf explained what the dream meant. Seven years of good harvests were coming, and the grain should be left in the ear. Seven hard years would follow, when people would live on those stores. Then a year of rain would bring relief (12:47-49).

The king sent for him, but Yūsuf wanted his innocence made clear first (12:50). The Prophet ﷺ praised this patience: “Had I stayed in prison as long as Yūsuf stayed, I would have answered the one who called me” (al-Bukhārī, no. 3372, and Muslim, no. 151).

The ʿAzīz’s wife confessed: “It was I who tried to seduce him, and he is telling the truth.” The king made him his close adviser. Later, at Yūsuf’s own request, he put him in charge of the country’s storehouses (12:54-56).

His brothers come back: “No blame on you today”

During the hard years, Yaʿqūb’s sons came to Egypt to buy grain. Yūsuf recognised them, but they didn’t recognise him (12:58). He asked them to come back with the brother who had stayed at home with their father (12:59).

Yaʿqūb hesitated, having already lost Yūsuf, but in the end he agreed (12:64-66). In Egypt, Yūsuf took this brother aside and told him: “I am your brother. Do not be sad.” Then he had the king’s cup hidden in his brother’s bag. By the brothers’ own rule, whoever had the cup had to stay behind. In this way, Yūsuf kept his brother with him (12:70-76).

The others went home without him. Once again Yaʿqūb met the news with beautiful patience (12:83), but his grief for Yūsuf turned his eyes white (12:84). He said: “I complain of my grief to Allah alone.” Then he sent his sons back to look for Yūsuf and his brother, and he never lost hope in Allah’s mercy (12:87).

When the brothers stood before Yūsuf in Egypt once more, he asked them what they had done to Yūsuf and his brother (12:89). The truth dawned on them: “Are you Yūsuf?” He answered: “I am Yūsuf, and this is my brother.” They admitted they had done wrong (12:91), and Yūsuf said to them:

قَالَ لَا تَثۡرِيبَ عَلَيۡكُمُ ٱلۡيَوۡمَۖ يَغۡفِرُ ٱللَّهُ لَكُمۡۖ وَهُوَ أَرۡحَمُ ٱلرَّٰحِمِينَ

“No blame on you today. May Allah forgive you. He is the most merciful of all who show mercy.”

He gave them his shirt to take to their father. When it was laid over Yaʿqūb’s face, his sight returned (12:93-96). His sons asked him to seek Allah’s forgiveness for them, and he promised he would (12:97-98).

The whole family came to Egypt. Yūsuf seated his parents on the throne, and they all bowed before him. The commentators say this was a greeting of respect at the time. Yūsuf said: “Father, this is the meaning of my dream of long ago.” The eleven stars were his brothers, and the sun and the moon were his parents.

In that moment of joy, Yūsuf mentioned the prison, but not the well. He said only that Satan had caused a rift “between me and my brothers”. The commentator as-Saʿdī sees this as complete forgiveness, without a single word of reproach.

What the surah does not say

The surah doesn’t name Yūsuf’s brothers or the ʿAzīz’s wife. It doesn’t give Yūsuf’s age, the colour of his shirt or how long he spent in the well. The names and details you may read elsewhere come from later accounts that can’t be traced back to any reliable witness. This article keeps to the Quran and to authentic hadiths, and so does our article on the story of Surah Al-Fīl.

In the Nūr app, the Stories tell one part of this surah: the dream, the well and the shirt. You’ll find it under the title “The shirt and the wolf”.

sources.ref: Qur'an, Sūrat Yūsuf (12:3-101). Arabic of 12:4 and 12:92 copied by script from Nūr's app text (src/data/quran-text.json, key "12"). Meanings: plain renderings written for this article, checked against the meaning the app quotes for sūrah 12 (Rachid Maach FR, Saheeh International EN, via QuranEnc, src/data/verseTable.json).
Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3390 (Ibn ʿUmar: الْكَرِيمُ ابْنُ الْكَرِيمِ ابْنِ الْكَرِيمِ ابْنِ الْكَرِيمِ يُوسُفُ بْنُ يَعْقُوبَ بْنِ إِسْحَاقَ بْنِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ)
Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3372 (Abū Hurayrah: "If I were to stay in prison for such a long time as Joseph did I would have accepted the offer")
Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 151a (Abū Hurayrah: "had I stayed (in the prison) as long as Yusuf stayed, I would have responded to him who invited me")
"Beautiful patience" glossed: Mujāhid (no panic) in aṭ-Ṭabarī; as-Saʿdī on 12:18 (free of resentment and of complaining to people). RESEARCH-YUSUF-SOURCES-189.md, table row 24, not re-fetched

The dream's meaning (stars = brothers, sun and moon = parents): Ibn Kathīr on 12:4 from Ibn ʿAbbās, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatādah and others; confirmed by 12:100. RESEARCH-YUSUF-SOURCES-189.md §1, not re-fetched
The bowing in 12:100 as a greeting of respect, lawful before the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: Saheeh International's footnote. RESEARCH-YUSUF-SOURCES-189.md §9, not re-fetched
as-Saʿdī on 12:100: Yūsuf names the prison and not the well, "out of his complete forgiveness of his brothers". RESEARCH-YUSUF-SOURCES-189.md §10, not re-fetched

notes:
§7 CHECK 1 True: every event is a verse of Sūrat Yūsuf, cited by number; the three hadiths were opened on sunnah.com today; the commentators' glosses come from RESEARCH-YUSUF-SOURCES-189.md and are said as theirs. The app claim ("La chemise et le loup" / "The shirt and the wolf" tells the dream, the well and the shirt) is read from stories.json, same text in the worktree and in master.
§7 CHECK 2 Within limit: the build script prints the counts. Titles and metas are the research file's own (§4.7), recounted by script. ex under 120. Body 800 to 1,200 words in each language (script count, Arabic excluded).
§7 CHECK 3 No banned word: scanned by script for meilleur/best, bienfaits, découvr-, gratuit, télécharge, pour enfants/for kids, tajwīd, Ṣalāh/prière/prayer/pray, relu par des savants. None. (12:3's « le plus beau des récits » / "the most beautiful of stories" is the verse's own phrase, kept away from "best".)
§7 CHECK 4 The whole of Nūr: n/a for an article that serves one door. Its last sentence names the Histoires and says the app tells only one part of the sūrah.
§7 CHECK 5 Reads alone: the five H2s are the research file's, in its order, without their verse ranges (the ranges carried en dashes). I ADDED a sixth H2, « Ce que la sourate ne dit pas », because the lane brief asks every article to say what was left out and why, in one plain paragraph. Drop it if Ahmed wants §4.7's five exactly.
§7 CHECK 6 Plain, no AI markers: no em or en dash anywhere (verse ranges use a hyphen), no either-or or from-to frame, no « découvrir », no semicolon, every term glossed at first use (sourate, Youssouf/Yūsuf/Joseph, Yacoub/Jacob, Ibrahim/Abraham, Ishaq/Isaac, hadith, ʿAzīz, belle patience). 12:4's prostration is rendered « s'incliner jusqu'au sol » so it needs no gloss. Sentence length varied by hand.
§7 CHECK 7 Voice: one adult to another, no children assumed, no guilt and no fear. The brothers are never shamed: the sūrah's own end (12:91-100) and as-Saʿdī's reading close the story on forgiveness. The tempting scene (12:23-29) is told plainly, for an adult, and goes no further than the verses.
§7 CHECK 8 French first: the French was written first; the English is derived, not word for word (en-GB: favour, colour, travellers; "Quran"). Names: Youssouf and Yacoub in French as the app writes them; Yūsuf and Yaʿqūb in English as the app writes them; "Yusuf" only in the English title and meta, the searched form.
§7 CHECK 9 Qur'an exact: the Arabic of 12:4 and 12:92 copied by script from quran-text.json; nothing typed.
PLAINNESS (RECIPE-STORIES §1 step 7), writer's pass done item by item: each verb carries its object; each person introduced where first met (Yacoub, the unnamed brother, the brother who objects, the ʿAzīz, his wife, the two prisoners, the king, the eldest); "this brother" is named as another son of Yacoub; time jumps said ("Un jour", "plusieurs années", "Pendant les années dures"); no verse cut with an ellipsis; each cause told (the jealousy, the shirt test, why he waits to leave prison, why the cup is hidden, how the father sees again); the dream's meaning is given at the end, where the sūrah gives it; the last section carries the main point (patience and forgiveness without reproach). NOT DONE: no fresh newcomer reader was run and plain.py was not run (it gates story drafts, not articles). Worth one newcomer read before it ships.
SENS SPANS (FR and EN, the same 18 each): 12:3, 12:4, 12:5, 12:8, 12:15, 12:18, 12:19, 12:23, 12:31, 12:33, 12:51, 12:69, 12:86, 12:90 (twice), 12:92, 12:100 (twice). Verses told in narration rather than quoted are cited by number in brackets and carry no span. 12:4 and 12:92 are also printed whole in Arabic.
TRANSLATION: the sens lines are my own plain renderings, not a published translation. For sūrah 12 the app quotes QuranEnc's Rachid Maach (FR) and Saheeh International (EN), whose terms forbid modification, so I did not adapt them; I read them only to check each sense. If Ahmed prefers, those QuranEnc texts can be quoted unchanged with their credit line. Note: Rachid Maach's 12:69 adds the name "Benjamin", which this article must not print, another reason not to quote it here. RESEARCH-YUSUF-SOURCES-189 read Saheeh International (quran.com 20) as research only, for 12:1-22 and parts of 12:31-101; verses 12:21-12:88 were rendered from the Arabic and the QuranEnc texts in verseTable.json.
LEFT OUT, and why: the names of the brothers, of the brother Yūsuf kept and of the ʿAzīz's wife, and any later marriage (later tradition, no chain; the Qur'an says only « la femme du ʿAzīz » and « son frère »); Yūsuf's age, the shirt's colour, the days in the well, the untorn shirt (Ibn ʿAbbās and others in aṭ-Ṭabarī, chains ungraded), the talking wolf, Jibrīl in the well, the stars' names (al-Ḥakam ibn Ẓuhayr, abandoned); "patience with no complaint" as the Prophet's ﷺ words (mursal, unknown narrator); Ibn Kathīr's other beauty reports (ungraded); Muslim 162a ("given half of beauty"), sound and checked, but optional in §4.7 and cut to stay under 1,200 words; 12:24's "he would have inclined to her" and 12:28's "your plotting is great" (summarised away, not needed for the plot); 12:41's two meanings (one man freed, the other put to death and the birds): summarised as "il explique leurs rêves", for length and to keep the death out; 12:52-53 (who speaks is disputed); 12:67's advice on the gates and 12:77's accusation (not needed); 12:101's prayer (not needed). Bukhārī 4690 (ʿĀʾishah and "beautiful patience") is sound but its context is the slander, so it stays out.
